findings.headline: Middlesbrough College investment will generate no rental income, contrary to prior expectations

findings.matters: Pre-allocating internal capital funds based on unconfirmed external contributions exposes the council to a funding gap if the external contribution is delayed or does not arrive.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Revenue and Capital Budget Quarter One 2026-27
findings.headline: Total unachievable or delayed savings reached £2.845m in 2026/27, with largest failures in corporate procurement and contract reviews (£0.619m)
findings.detail: Against a required £9.040m savings programme for 2026/27, the council has only achieved £6.195m, leaving £2.845m unachievable. The largest unachievable element is corporate savings: £0.619m in procurement and contract reviews and £0.200m in digitisation of procurement activity, 'largely due to the majority of savings that have been identified to date being unable to be realised as actual revenue budget savings as they have largely been related to capital expenditure.' These corporate savings will be 'reviewed as part of the budget setting process for 2027/28.'
findings.matters: Repeated failure to deliver cross-cutting corporate savings (this is on top of the £3.833m Children's Services savings abandoned) suggests systematic difficulty in delivering transformation programmes. A lender would see this as reduced confidence in management's ability to land planned efficiencies.
findings.figures: Total savings target 2026/27: £9.040m; achieved/budgeted adjustment: £6.195m; unachieved: £2.845m; corporate procurement savings £0.619m unachievable; digitisation £0.200m unachievable.
findings.quote: Despite best endeavours some remaining corporate savings are expected to be unachieved in the manner originally intended, comprising of £0.619m relating to Procurement and Contract Reviews, and £0.200m relating to digitisation of procurement activity. This is largely due to the majority of savings that have been identified to date being unable to be realised as actual revenue budget savings as they have largely been related to capital expenditure.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Revenue and Capital Budget Quarter One 2026-27
findings.headline: Long-term borrowing rates have risen to 5.40–5.70% for the 10–15 year period, above the council's 4.75% target, forcing reliance on short-term debt
findings.detail: The council's preferred long-term borrowing tenor (10–15 years) now costs 5.40–5.70%, well above the budgeted 4.75% rate due to 'global economic uncertainty.' As a result, the council is 'only taking short-term borrowing at rates between 4–4.25%' to finance capital and revenue needs. The council is currently 'under-borrowed' by £48.369m (14.5%) against its Capital Financing Requirement and 'may require around £50m additional borrowing over the remainder of the financial year.' This increases refinancing risk if short-term rates stay high or if the council needs to roll over debt at maturity.
findings.matters: Rising long-term rates increase the future cost of borrowing to fund the capital programme. Reliance on short-term debt creates refinancing risk if the council needs to roll debt over at higher rates. A lender would see this as pressure on future debt service costs.
findings.figures: PWLB rates 5.40–5.70% (10–15 years); budget target 4.75%; short-term rates taken 4–4.25%; under-borrowed position £48.369m (14.5%); potential additional borrowing need £50m; capital financing cost forecast £13.651m (6.8% of revenue budget).
findings.quote: Long-term interest rates from the Public Works Loan Board have continued to increase due to the global economic uncertainty because of the Iran War. These are now around 5.40% – 5.70% in the 10–15-year period which has been the preferred option for external long-term borrowing in recent years. This is well above the target borrowing rate of 4.75% for the financial year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Revenue and Capital Budget Quarter One 2026-27
findings.headline: Environment and Communities is forecasting a £1.342m overspend driven by income shortfalls in property, planning, parking and cultural services

Planning income is delayed because 'major planning applications' submissions are delayed 'dependent upon developer activity'. These are described as 'structural challenges facing local government.'
findings.matters: Income-sensitive budgets (property, planning, parking, culture) are harder to control and more vulnerable to economic slowdown. A lender would see declining town centre footfall and commercial property occupancy as warning signals about the council's economic territory.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Revenue and Capital Budget Quarter One 2026-27
findings.headline: £3.833m of Children's Services savings carried forward from previous years are being formally abandoned as no longer achievable in their intended form
findings.detail: These savings were from 'historic transformation projects' including internal residential, workforce development, maximising grants, modernising foster care and edge of care. Although the budgets were reduced in these areas, 'the original assumptions underpinning the savings are no longer valid and it is no longer possible to demonstrate delivery through the intended projects.' The council notes this 'reduced budget provision in these areas is likely to continue to contribute towards future budget pressures and forecast overspends.'
findings.matters: Formally abandoning historic savings signals either that past transformation programmes failed or that the environment has changed fundamentally. This reduces confidence in whether current recovery plans will land, and warns that 'savings' may need to be re-scoped in future years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Revenue and Capital Budget Quarter One 2026-27
findings.headline: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit is forecast to reach £38.316m by March 2027, with a £9.000m in-year overspend in the High Needs Block
findings.detail: The cumulative DSG deficit exists because of sustained demand and complexity in special educational needs. Although held separately from the General Fund under statutory override (extended to March 2028), it represents a significant contingent liability. The council's access to a High Needs Stability Grant depends on successful Department for Education approval of its Local SEND Reform Plan, 'which is currently going through the Secretary of State approval process' with results expected September 2026. The reform plan 'provides a route towards longer-term sustainability' but DSG 'remains a significant financial risk.'
findings.matters: A £38m contingent liability is material even if separately accounted for. It signals sustained structural demand pressure in a protected budget, and the council's financial recovery depends on government approvals that are not yet guaranteed.
findings.figures: Cumulative DSG deficit forecast at 31/03/27: £38.316m; in-year overspend 2026/27: £9.000m (High Needs Block £9.000m); balance at 31/03/26 was £29.316m so increase of £9m in one year.
findings.quote: The forecast cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit is expected to increase to £38.316m by March 2027. Whilst national reforms and the Local SEND Reform Plan (still to be approved by the DfE), provide a route towards longer-term sustainability, DSG remains a significant financial risk for the Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Revenue and Capital Budget Quarter One 2026-27
findings.headline: Children's Social Care is forecasting an £8.472m overspend, representing 100% of the council's total budget pressure
findings.detail: The overspend is driven primarily by agency staffing (£3.788m), external residential placements (£2.575m), and increasing numbers of children looked after. The service has undertaken an Ofsted ILACS inspection. The council recognises 'the severity of the current forecast position and the need for urgent action.' Recovery actions have been identified but 'the financial impact has not yet been fully quantified', so the forecast 'does not assume any significant reduction from future recovery actions.'
findings.matters: Children's services overspends are driven by statutory demand and placement costs, making them harder to control than discretionary services. A lender would need to understand whether this is temporary or structural, and whether the council can realistically manage it.
findings.figures: £8.472m overspend; agency £3.788m; external placements £2.575m; Children with Disabilities £0.409m. Numbers of children looked after have 'continued to increase' compared to same period previous year.
findings.quote: Children's Social Care is forecasting a significant budget pressure at Quarter One, primarily driven by continued reliance on agency staffing, high-cost external residential placements and Independent Fostering Agency placements, together with increasing numbers of children looked after.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F2 - Details of savings classified as unachievable
findings.headline: The council cannot reduce agency staffing costs by £0.380m because it cannot recruit to permanent posts and demand remains high.
findings.detail: Service demand pressures combined with recruitment failure mean the council cannot replace agency staff with permanent posts, preventing the budgeted agency cost reduction.
findings.matters: This is a structural issue in the labour market that the council cannot control. It shows whether the budget assumption of stable demand and successful recruitment was realistic.
findings.figures: £0.380m unachievable (CS04)
findings.quote: Service demand pressures and the inability to recruit to permanent posts is preventing the ability to achieve this target.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F2 - Details of savings classified as unachievable
findings.headline: The council is delaying a £0.615m investment in expanding internal residential children's homes because staffing difficulties and Ofsted concerns are blocking the project.
findings.detail: The Ofsted improvement plan is a prerequisite for proceeding with capacity expansion in internal residential homes. Staffing recruitment and quality assurance problems mean the council cannot safely commit to this investment until the improvement plan is embedded and proven.
findings.matters: This signals children's services is in improvement (Ofsted intervention) and the council cannot rely on planned capital investment to manage demand. It limits flexibility in cost control.
findings.figures: £0.615m delayed (CC03)
findings.quote: Due to difficulties in staffing in residential care and limited assurance on quality of care, it proposed to delay increasing capacity in internal residential homes until the Ofsted Improvement plan is embedded

findings.paper_title: Appendix F2 - Details of savings classified as unachievable
findings.headline: The council approved £0.819m in procurement savings that cannot now be achieved because the identified savings were capital expenditure, not revenue budget savings.
findings.detail: The council merged two initiatives (contract spend review and digitised procurement activity) totalling £0.819m. Budget setting assumed these would produce revenue savings but work has revealed most of the identified savings relate to capital expenditure and cannot be realised as revenue budget reductions as originally intended.
findings.matters: This reveals a planning error in budget-setting where capital savings were mistaken for revenue savings. It signals governance and budget monitoring weakness at the point of approval, and the council has no mitigation plan.
findings.figures: £0.819m unachievable (FIN13, merged from FIN07 £0.619m and FIN12 £0.200m)
findings.quote: Despite best endeavours, it has now become apparent that the remainder of these savings cannot now be achieved in the manner originally intended. This is largely due to the majority of savings that have been identified to date being unable to be realised as actual revenue budget savings as they have largely been related to capital expenditure.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F2 - Details of savings classified as unachievable
findings.headline: A national temporary accommodation crisis is directly preventing the council from reducing emergency housing spending by £0.200m.
findings.detail: The council planned to coordinate housing provision to reduce emergency and temporary accommodation costs. This saving is now unachievable because demand for temporary accommodation has become a national crisis that is out of the council's control.
findings.matters: This is an external demand shock hitting the council's budget. Lenders need to understand whether this is temporary or structural, and whether it signals a deteriorating social care or homelessness position in the area.
findings.figures: £0.200m unachievable saving from REG07 (total plan £0.500m)
findings.quote: A national crisis in temporary accommodation is impacting the ability of adults and children's directorate's ability to achieve remaining saving.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F2 - Details of savings classified as unachievable
findings.headline: Children's Care is failing to achieve £1.483m of budgeted savings due to high numbers in care and staffing crises.
findings.detail: The council planned five separate savings totalling £5.316m in Children's Care but has now marked £1.483m (28%) as unachievable. The Edge of Care team, intended to reduce children in care, has not translated into actual savings despite costing avoidance efforts. Ofsted improvement plan requirements are delaying residential capacity expansion. Foster care cooperation with the regional scheme cannot deliver savings as planned.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's financial control needs to know whether Children's Care demand (which is cost-driven) can actually be managed down, or whether this is a structural budget pressure that will persist.
findings.figures: £1.483m unachieved out of £5.316m planned; CC10 £0.400m, CC08 £0.368m, CC03 £0.615m, CC05 £0.100m
findings.quote: Number of children in care remains high. The team have been successful in cost avoidance however this has not translated to overall savings against base budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F4 - Dedicated Schools Grant
findings.headline: DSG deficit remains classified as unusable reserve until March 2028, converting then to usable reserves.
findings.detail: Currently the deficit sits as an unusable reserve (not available to spend), but the government framework allows this to revert to usable status from 31 March 2028. This timing affects the council's apparent reserve position and when the council can draw on them for other purposes.
findings.matters: Lenders track usable reserves as a key measure of financial resilience. This timetable means the council's reserve picture will materially change in 2028, and the council's MTFP must account for this.

findings.quote: The remaining deficit will continue to be reported as unusable reserve until 31 March 2028 when the balance will revert to be reported as usable council reserves.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F4 - Dedicated Schools Grant
findings.headline: DSG deficit has spillover impact on General Fund through home-to-school transport costs.
findings.detail: The document explicitly notes that transport pressures sit outside the ring-fenced DSG and are funded from the council's core budget, meaning the SEND crisis is not fully contained within the schools grant.
findings.matters: The true cost to the council's financial position is larger than the DSG deficit alone. A lender assessing reserves and General Fund pressure needs to account for transport and other spillover costs.
findings.figures: None specified in the paper.
findings.quote: These demand pressures also have a wider financial impact, particularly on home to school transport costs, which are funded from the Councils core budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F4 - Dedicated Schools Grant
findings.headline: EHCP demand has grown 22% in three years (1,669 to 2,040) and plan approval is the key lever for controlling future growth.
findings.detail: The council identifies demand pressures as structural — rising EHCPs, complexity of need, and specialist placements — with the Local SEND Reform Plan relying on reduced demand through mainstream inclusion and early intervention. The plan explicitly recognises the risk that if these measures do not deliver at pace, the financial position will not improve.
findings.matters: Demand control is the only path to sustainability. If inclusion and early intervention do not work, pressure on the High Needs Block will continue and the council's financial position will worsen.
findings.figures: EHCPs increased from 1,669 in 2022 to over 2,040 in 2025.
findings.quote: Continued growth in EHCP's, increasing from 1,669 in 2022 to over 2,040 in 2025.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F4 - Dedicated Schools Grant
findings.headline: DSG deficit dependent on Secretary of State approval of Local SEND Reform Plan by September/October 2026, with conditional 90% government coverage.
findings.detail: The High Needs Block deficit is covered up to 90% by a new High Needs Stability Grant announced February 2026, but only if the council's Local SEND Reform Plan is approved. The risk of non-approval or slow delivery would leave the council without this funding source and force the deficit into usable reserves from 2028.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether this deficit is supported or not. Plan rejection would materially worsen the council's reserve position and financial flexibility.
findings.figures: 90% of DSG deficits accumulated at 31 March 2026; remaining deficit reverts to usable reserves 31 March 2028.
findings.quote: a High Needs Stability Grant, which will cover up to 90% of DSG deficits accumulated at 31 March 2026, subject to plan approval.

findings.paper_title: Audit Strategy Memorandum - Middlesbrough Council
findings.headline: Prior-year audit concerns about capital accounting interpretation remain unresolved
findings.detail: The auditor identified concerns during prior-year work about how the council interprets CIPFA Code requirements on capital accounting. These concerns have not yet been fully addressed and require attention as part of this year's audit.
findings.matters: Incorrect application of capital accounting rules can result in misstated asset valuations and depreciation expense, potentially overstating the council's asset base or distorting historical financial position.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: As part of the previous year's financial statement work, we identified and reported concerns around the Council's interpretation of the CIPFA Code relating to capital accounting which needed to be addressed.

findings.paper_title: Audit Strategy Memorandum - Middlesbrough Council
findings.headline: Debtors impairment of £28.4 million under enhanced audit scrutiny, signalling collection risks
findings.detail: The auditor identifies the council's impairment allowance for debtors as an enhanced audit risk requiring critical review of the calculation methodology and disclosure compliance, indicating significant doubt over collectability of amounts owed.
findings.matters: A £28.4m impairment provision representing uncollectable debt signals weak revenue collection in key income streams or deteriorating debtor circumstances, threatening cash receipts.
findings.figures: £28.4 million impairment of debtors' allowance as at 31 March 2025

findings.paper_title: Audit Strategy Memorandum - Middlesbrough Council
findings.headline: Finance team capacity remains inadequate, threatening ability to prepare compliant financial statements
findings.detail: The auditor explicitly flags continuing gaps in capacity within the finance team and recent personnel changes as a concern affecting the council's ability to prepare Code-compliant financial statements, particularly given the complexity of the rebuilding assurance process.
findings.matters: Understaffed finance functions increase risk of financial reporting errors, missed deadlines, control failures, and inability to manage complex accounting or crisis situations.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: Our planning and risk assessment work will consider whether the issues identified lead to concerns about the Council's arrangements for preparing Code compliant financial statements given the continuing gaps in capacity in the finance team and other changes in the team.

findings.paper_title: Audit Strategy Memorandum - Middlesbrough Council
findings.headline: Audit fee increasing 73% from prior year, signalling substantially elevated complexity and risk
findings.detail: The proposed audit fee for 2025/26 is £361,966, up from £208,928 in 2024/25 (which was itself only 60% of full scale fee). The significant increase reflects the auditor's assessment of materially more complex and higher-risk audit work required.
findings.matters: Rising audit fees correlate with deteriorating financial control environments and increased risk of material misstatement, often accompanying financial stress or governance weakness.
findings.figures: 2024-25 actual fee: £208,928 (60% of scale fee); 2025-26 proposed: £361,966
findings.quote: Statutory audit work to comply with the NAO Code of Audit Practice £361,966 [2025-26]; £208,928 [2024-25]

findings.paper_title: Audit Strategy Memorandum - Middlesbrough Council
findings.headline: Audit opinions remain disclaimed for third consecutive year; full assurance not expected until 2027/28
findings.detail: The council received disclaimed audit opinions for both 2023/24 and 2024/25 because the auditor could not complete all required procedures before statutory deadlines. The rebuilding assurance strategy means opinions will remain modified through 2026/27, with full unmodified opinion not expected until 2027/28 at earliest.
findings.matters: Disclaimed opinions mean neither the council nor external stakeholders have reasonable assurance that financial statements are accurate, creating fundamental uncertainty over the true financial position, asset valuations, and reserve balances.

findings.quote: On 3 March 2026, we disclaimed our opinion on the Council's 2024/25 financial statements. This followed on from disclaimed opinions issued previously in respect of the Council's 2023/2024 accounts. We issued a disclaimer of opinion because there was not sufficient time to complete all required audit procedures in advance of the backstop date to enable us to form an opinion on the financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Audit Strategy Memorandum - Middlesbrough Council
findings.headline: Council continues to rely on exceptional government financial support to achieve a balanced budget
findings.detail: The auditor identifies as a continuing significant weakness that the council remains dependent on Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) from government to set a balanced budget, rather than achieving financial balance through in-year management and savings.
findings.matters: Structural reliance on one-off government bailouts indicates the council cannot live within permanent funding levels and suggests underlying cost control or service delivery problems that will recur annually.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: The Council is still reliant on EFS to set a balanced budget.

findings.paper_title: Audit Strategy Memorandum - Middlesbrough Council
findings.headline: DSG deficit projected to reach £55 million within three years with insufficient reserves to cover it
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant (schools funding) deficit has grown from £14m in 2024/25 to £22m in the current year and is projected to reach £55m within three years. The auditor explicitly identifies this as a significant weakness in financial sustainability arrangements because the council lacks sufficient usable reserves to cover this expenditure gap.
findings.matters: A £55m structural funding gap in schools spending is an existential financial threat that signals potential inability to meet statutory education obligations without major service cuts or further government intervention.
findings.figures: DSG deficit increased from £14 million (2024/25) to £22 million (current year); projected to reach £55 million within three years
findings.quote: The Council's DSG deficit has increased in 2024/25 from £14 million to £22 million. Based on current Council projections as at September 2025, the deficit will increase to £55 million in the next three years. The DSG deficit is an indicator of a significant risk to financial sustainability because the Council does not have sufficient usable reserves to cover the potential expenditure needed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Details of savings classified as unachievable in 2025-26
findings.headline: Education & Partnerships savings pushed to 2026-27 with admission of unrealistic timescales.
findings.detail: Middlesbrough has re-profiled £0.345m of education savings from 2025-26 into 2026-27, with explicit acknowledgement that original delivery plans were based on unrealistic timescales. The delayed initiatives include passenger assistance training (£0.037m), transport capacity increases (£0.084m), management review (£0.044m), discretionary home-to-school transport recharge (£0.078m), and travel training (£0.102m).
findings.matters: Timing slippage of planned savings creates budget gaps in the current year. The explicit admission of unrealistic timescales suggests forecasting discipline issues within the education directorate.
findings.figures: £0.345m total: passenger assistance training £0.037m, transport capacity £0.084m, management review £0.044m, discretionary transport recharge £0.078m, travel training £0.102m
findings.quote: The majority of the budgeted savings are unachieved to date in 2025/26. Plans for achievement or replacement savings to be reprofiled to reflect more realistic delivery timescales, incorporated into the 2026/27 base budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Details of savings classified as unachievable in 2025-26
findings.headline: Procurement savings miscalculated: £1.519m double-counted and capital savings wrongly coded as revenue.
findings.detail: A procurement contract management saving (FIN13) of £1.519m has been removed from the 2025-26 revenue savings target. The savings represent a double-count from the prior year budget-setting cycle, and additional savings achieved were on capital contracts rather than revenue spending, making them unable to offset the revenue target shortfall. The council has revised its Medium-Term Financial Plan to reflect reduced procurement savings.
findings.matters: Accounting errors in tracking savings undermine lender confidence in the council's understanding of its own financial position and budget management discipline.
findings.figures: £1.519m double-counted from FIN07 (prior year); capital vs revenue classification error
findings.quote: Double count of saving FIN07 from 24/25 budget setting. In addition savings achieved to date have been in respect of Capital Contracts and therefore unable to allocate against the revenue savings target for 25/26. These savings have been reviewed through the Medium-Term Financial Plan and have been reduced.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Details of savings classified as unachievable in 2025-26
findings.headline: Homelessness demand surge preventing cost savings; council flags need for permanent replacement saving.
findings.detail: A planned £0.300m saving from improved coordination of emergency, temporary, and short-term housing has not materialised because homeless case numbers are increasing. The council acknowledges that increased demand means the initiative will only produce cost reduction rather than actual budget savings, and has flagged this shortfall will require a permanent replacement saving elsewhere.
findings.matters: This signals demand-driven cost growth the council cannot control or offset through coordination alone. The explicit need for permanent replacement saving means the £0.300m must be found elsewhere in the budget.
findings.figures: £0.300m unachieved
findings.quote: Whilst there are actions being undertaken which will address costs, the nature of the budgets which sit within other directorates and the increase in homeless cases will only result in cost reduction rather than budget savings. This saving will be replaced permanently by an alternative saving.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Details of savings classified as unachievable in 2025-26
findings.headline: Grant-writing capacity lost; Children's Services bid writer post vacant with £0.604m grant funding unachieved.
findings.detail: Middlesbrough's Maximising Grants initiative in Children's Services has failed to achieve £0.604m of savings because the bid writer post has left the council. The council is awaiting outcomes on two pending bids but has lost internal expertise for pursuing new grant opportunities.
findings.matters: Loss of grant-writing capacity signals organizational retention issues and reduces the council's ability to access external funding that offsets service costs.
findings.figures: £0.604m unachieved
findings.quote: Bid writer post has left. Currently awaiting outcome of two bids and any impact if successful on 2025-26 financial position.

findings.headline: Children's residential care placements rising despite multiple cost-control initiatives.
findings.detail: Middlesbrough has failed to achieve £3.2m of planned savings from initiatives designed to reduce expensive residential child placements. The Modernising Foster Care programme (£1.518m) aimed to increase fostering and reduce residential use but demand and placement complexity have driven increased residential care use instead. The Edge of Care Team (£0.800m) has not reduced placement numbers and placements are increasing rather than decreasing. A staffing review (£0.500m) and agency cost controls (£0.380m) have also not landed as planned.

findings.quote: While initiatives to increase fostering provision and reduce residential placements are in progress, demand and placememt complexity have continued to drive increased use of residential care in-year

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Strategic Risk Register Progress at Year-End 2025-26
findings.headline: Children's safeguarding improvement remains above safe levels with government intervention risk and OFSTED inspection due
findings.detail: Children's safeguarding quality practice remains a risk (score 21, target 10), well above acceptable levels. The council is subject to ongoing OFSTED monitoring with a focused visit due in the current fiscal year. Government intervention risk is explicitly mentioned if quality practice is not achieved. The council is relying on an improvement board and enhanced audit activity.
findings.matters: Ongoing safeguarding weakness that triggers government intervention risk signals systemic management problems and creates potential for service disruption or imposed action.

findings.quote: If the Council fails to deliver quality practice within children's safeguarding services then this may result in further government intervention, serious harm to individuals and loss of financial control.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Strategic Risk Register Progress at Year-End 2025-26
findings.headline: Tees Valley Combined Authority governance has not improved and remains at maximum risk despite Best Value Inspection Notice
findings.detail: TVCA governance risk has not improved at all—it remains at score 35, the maximum possible, with no movement toward the target of 14. A Best Value Inspection Notice was issued in April 2025, indicating formal government oversight of governance failure. The council notes that TVCA's governance arrangements are 'not fit for purpose' and are creating barriers to collaboration and hindering Middlesbrough's strategic ambitions. This governance failure is directly harming the council's ability to operate effectively.
findings.matters: A key partner authority (whose board Middlesbrough sits on) is under formal government inspection for governance failure. This limits the council's regional influence and creates partnership risk.
findings.figures: Score: original 35, current 35, target 14. Best Value Inspection Notice issued April 2025.
findings.quote: The governance arrangements of the Combined Authority (CA) are not fit for purpose, creating barriers to effective collaboration with the Council and adversely impacting the Council's ability to achieve its ambitions for the town.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Strategic Risk Register Progress at Year-End 2025-26
findings.headline: Children's social care is the single biggest financial viability risk and remains above safe levels
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies volatile demand and cost of children's social care as the single biggest risk to overall financial viability. Current score is 28, still well above the target of 21. Weekly financial monitoring and placement reviews are in place, but the risk trajectory suggests cost pressures are not being controlled within budget.
findings.matters: A service that the council identifies as its largest threat to viability is a material credit risk; escalating social care costs are driving deficits across English councils and indicate structural budget problems.
findings.figures: Score: original 35, current 28, target 21. Weekly financial monitoring ongoing.
findings.quote: The risk that demand and cost of and children's social care continues to escalate on the scale experienced in 2024/25, is the single biggest risk to the Councils financial viability.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - Strategic Risk Register Progress at Year-End 2025-26
findings.headline: DSG deficit threatens reserves depletion and section 114 notice if statutory override expires without government solution
findings.detail: The statutory override that allows High Needs Funding Deficit to be carried forward expired on 31 March 2026. If no national solution materializes, Middlesbrough must meet the DSG shortfall from general fund reserves. The council projects this will exhaust reserves entirely, triggering a potential section 114 notice (financial emergency). The risk remains at score 15, above the target of 9, suggesting this remains unresolved three months after the deadline.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion and section 114 notices are existential financial events; this creates direct lending risk and signals the council may lose financial control.
findings.figures: Score: current 15, target 9. Deadline: 31 March 2026 (now passed).
findings.quote: Based upon the current projection of the DSG high needs deficit compared to the level of revenue reserves, this will result in the Council's reserves being exhausted and the Council's s151 Officer potentially being required to issue a s114 Notice.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Prudential Indicators 2026/27 to 2029/30 and Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: S151 Officer explicitly recommends reducing borrowing dependency in favour of grants and asset sales
findings.detail: The Corporate Director of Finance's assessment is that the council should prioritise securing capital financing through grants and asset sales rather than prudential borrowing, to 'minimise future borrowing.' This is a strategic shift driven by the affordability constraints above. Government grants are collapsing over the MTFP (from £34.3m in 2025/26 to £6.4m in 2027/28), forcing the council to become increasingly dependent on finite asset disposals (£22.2m forecast for 2026/27) to fund its capital programme.
findings.matters: This indicates the council is strategically retreating from borrowing-funded capital investment and becoming dependent on asset sales—a finite resource that eventually depletes. This constraint could lead to reduced public capital investment and service capability over time.
findings.quote: The Corporate Director of Finance's view is that the Council will still benefit from prioritising its capital investment decisions over the medium and longer term and should secure its financing through third party funds such as contributions and grants and capital receipts from the sale of assets to minimise future borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Prudential Indicators 2026/27 to 2029/30 and Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Council has reached the limit of its revenue affordability for borrowing and must reconsider appropriate thresholds
findings.detail: The document explicitly states the council 'was reaching the limit of its revenue affordability on borrowing to fund its future capital investment.' The council's CFR is rising 6.8% annually (reaching £333.8m by March 2027) while debt forecasts show ongoing increases. Following Fair Funding Review changes, the council must now review whether the previously CIPFA-recommended 10% financing cost threshold remains appropriate, indicating structural constraints on future borrowing capacity.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council has limited headroom to increase borrowing further and may face significant capital investment restrictions or be forced to prioritise debt service over services.
findings.figures: CFR increasing £21.4m (6.8%) in 2026/27; External debt forecast £326.1m by March 2027; Proportion of revenue 7.1% but previously could reach 10%
findings.quote: Whilst the Council is not an outlier in terms of its level of total debt, it was reaching the limit of its revenue affordability on borrowing to fund its future capital investment.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Prudential Indicators 2026/27 to 2029/30 and Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Commercial property rental income is essential to budget affordability and explicitly flagged as 'key budget risk'
findings.detail: The council's forecast financing cost ratio of 7.1% of revenue is dependent on maintaining £2.6m annual income from commercial property investments made for regeneration purposes. The document explicitly warns this rental income must be sustained or the budgeted affordability ratios will not hold. The absolute financing costs are rising (£12.2m to £14.2m) but appear affordable only because revenue budgets have increased dramatically due to Fair Funding Review changes.
findings.matters: A lender assessing debt service capacity needs to know the affordability ratios rest on assumptions vulnerable to property market downturns, tenant defaults, or underperforming regeneration investments.
findings.figures: £2.6m annual income vs £14.151m financing costs (2026/27); proportion of revenue 7.1%
findings.quote: It is imperative and a key budget risk that these rental levels are maintained, and the income assumed in the estimates above continue to be generated.

findings.paper_title: Prudential Indicators 2026/27 to 2029/30 and Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Capital programme described as requiring 'strict management and prioritisation' despite being technically affordable
findings.detail: While capital programme remains within revenue budget parameters, report emphasizes it 'needs to be strictly managed and prioritised going forward.' Council recommended to 'prioritise capital investment decisions over medium and longer term' and 'secure financing through third party funds such as contributions and grants and capital receipts from sale of assets to minimise future borrowing.'
findings.matters: Tight headroom suggests council may need to defer or abandon projects if receipts/grants fall short, or revenue pressures emerge elsewhere.
findings.figures: Authorised limit for external debt 2026/27: £354m (vs CFR £333.755m, creating £20m headroom)
findings.quote: The capital programme and financing being recommended in the budget report remains affordable within the revenue budget parameters but needs to be strictly managed and prioritised going forward.

findings.paper_title: Prudential Indicators 2026/27 to 2029/30 and Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Internal cash reserves funding capital investment are depleting rapidly; under-borrowed position falls from £23m to £2.7m by 2027/28
findings.detail: Council currently holds £23.023m of internal cash balances being used to finance capital without external borrowing. This cushion shrinks to £7.727m by 2026/27 and just £2.727m by 2027/28, exhausting the council's financial flexibility. After 2027/28 position shows modest recovery to £5–7.5m, but the trajectory shows rapid depletion through mid-decade.
findings.matters: Shrinking under-borrowed position means council will have minimal headroom to absorb unexpected capital needs, cash flow pressures, or refinancing challenges without forced borrowing or project deferrals.
findings.quote: The Council therefore has an expected under-borrowed position of £23.023 million, which is financed via internal cash balances and provides a level of savings in interest payments as other revenue and capital cash has been used in lieu of borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Prudential Indicators 2026/27 to 2029/30 and Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review 2.0 creates £57m accounting distortion, rendering pre-2026/27 comparisons meaningless
findings.detail: Net revenue budget jumps from £143.304m to £200.675m in 2026/27 due to how Fair Funding Review 2.0 recalculates this metric. Report explicitly states figures pre-2026/27 are 'not exactly comparable with those going forward.' This accounting cliff makes it impossible to trend the council's real fiscal health or assess whether debt service is actually lightening or just appears to be due to numerator/denominator shift.
findings.matters: Lenders cannot reliably assess debt trajectory or affordability trend across this structural accounting change; real fiscal pressure may be obscured by the funding methodology shift.
findings.figures: Net revenue budget 2025/26: £143.304m; 2026/27: £200.675m; Fair Funding Review 2.0 makes pre/post figures non-comparable
findings.quote: Changes to the Local Government Finance Settlement and how the net revenue budget have been calculated have changed significantly with the Fair Funding Review 2.0 and are not now comparable post the 2026/27 budget.

findings.paper_title: Prudential Indicators 2026/27 to 2029/30 and Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Council reached limit of revenue affordability for borrowing; reviewing whether 10% CIPFA threshold still applies
findings.detail: Capital Financing Requirement rising from £312.383m (2025/26) to £358.733m (2029/30). Financing costs rising from £12.205m to £17.396m over same period. Report explicitly states council was 'reaching the limit of revenue affordability on borrowing' and must review if 10% best-practice CIPFA threshold remains relevant given changed funding settlement.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know whether council can sustain this debt trajectory or if further borrowing will be constrained by its own affordability ceilings.
findings.figures: CFR £312.383m → £358.733m; Financing costs £12.205m → £17.396m; Debt service 8.5% of net revenue budget (2025/26)
findings.quote: it was reaching the limit of its revenue affordability on borrowing to fund its future capital investment

findings.paper_title: Middlesbrough Council Audit Completion Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Centre Square lease remeasurement (£2.262m) accounted for incorrectly under IFRS 16
findings.detail: The council has accounted for the £2.262m Centre Square lease remeasurement on transition to IFRS 16 as a donated asset added to investment properties. The auditor believes it should have been charged to the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement under Financing & Investment Activities as part of Movement in Fair Value, then reversed via Movement in Reserves.
findings.matters: Incorrect IFRS 16 treatment can obscure the true cost of leases and misstate both asset values and financing charges. This suggests the council may not have fully embedded the new leasing standard.
findings.figures: £2.262m remeasurement of Centre Square lease
findings.quote: The £2.262m remeasurement of the Centre Square lease on transition to IFRS 16 has been accounted for as a donated asset, so as an addition to the Investment Properties balance. However, in accordance with the CIPFA Code, this remeasurement adjustment should have been charged to the CIES, Financing & Investment Activities Expenditure

findings.paper_title: Middlesbrough Council Audit Completion Report 2024/25
findings.headline: IT control deficiencies identified: password management, privileged access, user access reviews
findings.detail: The auditor's IT testing identified weaknesses in password management, privileged access controls, and user access reviews. The auditor warns that lack of user controls increases the risk of unauthorized access to applications and may adversely impact the integrity and confidentiality of financially significant information.
findings.matters: Weak IT controls can allow unauthorized changes to financial records, data theft, or system compromise. This is a material control weakness affecting the reliability of financial information.
findings.figures: IT audit identified three areas needing improvement: password management, privileged access, user access reviews
findings.quote: The lack of user controls increases the risk of unauthorised access to the application and may adversely impact the integrity and confidentiality of financially significant information.

findings.paper_title: Middlesbrough Council Audit Completion Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Performance management arrangements lack clear links between council priorities and detailed targets
findings.detail: Although a new Council Plan 2024-27 has been developed outlining the Mayor's four priorities, the auditor identified a lack of evidence of clear links between these priorities, the strategic workplan, and detailed outcomes and measures reported. The auditor recommends ensuring the Mayor's priorities are clearly linked to the strategic workplan and feed into detailed, measurable targets and staff performance appraisals.
findings.matters: Without clear performance management linking strategy to delivery, the council cannot reliably demonstrate whether its spending is achieving intended outcomes. This weakens accountability and makes it harder to identify and fix underperformance.
findings.figures: Council Plan 2024-27 covers four Mayor priorities; VFM work identified lack of embedded links
findings.quote: Our work, however, identified a lack of evidence of a clear link between the Council Plan priorities in 2024/25, the strategic workplan and the detailed outcomes and measures reported.

findings.paper_title: Middlesbrough Council Audit Completion Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Council using collection data from 2012-1993 and 2013 to calculate bad debt provisions
findings.detail: The council calculates expected credit loss for council tax using the average collection rate for 2012-1993 (less 1%) and for business rates using 2013 data. The auditor has queried when this will be updated to a more recent date, noting that collection rates are decreasing. Officers have confirmed this is currently being reviewed.
findings.matters: Using collection data over 30 years old is unreliable and likely to understate bad debts if current collection performance is worse. This could overstate the value of debtors on the balance sheet.
findings.figures: Council tax: 2012-1993 average less 1%; Business rates: 2013 rate
findings.quote: The expected credit loss for council tax is calculated using the average collection rate for 2012-1993 less 1%. Similarly, for business rates, the 2013 rate has been used. We have queried at what point this will be updated to a more recent date as collection rates are decreasing.

findings.paper_title: Middlesbrough Council Audit Completion Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Investment property income and receipts misclassified across financial statements
findings.detail: £15.7m capital receipt from sale of an investment property was recorded in the wrong section of the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement (Other Operating rather than Financing). Additionally, £1.552m rental income and £0.877m operating expenses from investment properties were recorded in Regeneration line rather than Financing and Investment Activities.
findings.matters: Material misclassifications of investment income and receipts obscure the council's true operating performance and financing activity. These errors suggest weak controls over complex transactions.
findings.figures: £15.703m capital receipt (net of costs) from investment property disposal; £1.552m rental income; £0.877m direct operating expenses
findings.quote: The £15.703m capital receipt (net of costs) from the sale of an Investment Property has been included in the Other Operating I&E section of the CIES along with receipts from the sale of PPE and AHFS. However, per the Code Guidance Notes, the gain/loss on derecognition of Investment Property should be included in the Financing I&E section

findings.paper_title: Middlesbrough Council Audit Completion Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Multiple material capital accounting errors, including £21.7m adopted roads misclassification
findings.detail: Adopted roads have been recognized as donated assets valued at £40.5m gross (£21.7m net) based on historical developer costs. The auditor understands the Code requires these to be at nil consideration. Additionally, indexation of PPE has been applied incorrectly; one asset was revalued down from £7.8m to £4.7m but then indexed back up to £7.8m. The auditor found net errors of £0.171m in this area.
findings.matters: These are systemic errors in how the council capitalizes and values fixed assets. They reflect gaps in understanding of accounting standards. The £21.7m adopted roads issue alone is material and suggests the council's asset base may be overstated.
findings.figures: Adopted roads: gross book value £40.547m, net book value £21.666m. One asset opened at £7.8m, revalued to £4.7m, then indexed back to £7.8m. Overall error identified: £0.171m.
findings.quote: Adopted roads have been recognised as donated assets and valued using the historical costs included in the original development agreements. Our understanding of the Code is that generally accepted practice is to include these assets at nil consideration. Gross book value as at 31 March 2025 is £40.547m, net book value £21.666m.

findings.paper_title: Middlesbrough Council Audit Completion Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Significant and growing DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) deficit
findings.detail: The auditor identifies a significant and growing deficit in the council's schools funding. The council is directed to continue implementing initiatives to improve prevention, transform provision, reduce costs, and identify income to offset high needs spend.
findings.matters: A growing DSG deficit is typically sticky and hard to resolve. It puts pressure on the council's overall financial position and reduces flexibility to manage other pressures. The 'growing' nature suggests it is worsening.
findings.figures: Auditor report refers to 'significant and growing DSG deficit' but specific figures not disclosed in this section
findings.quote: The Council has a significant and growing DSG deficit.

findings.paper_title: Middlesbrough Council Audit Completion Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Council received exceptional financial support from government to balance 2024/25 budget
findings.detail: Middlesbrough made a formal request for and received emergency government funding to set a balanced budget in 2024/25. The auditor identifies this as evidence of a significant weakness in arrangements for planning to bridge funding gaps and identifying achievable savings. The auditor notes the approach has improved but needs more focus on underlying assumptions.
findings.matters: Reliance on emergency government funding signals the council cannot solve its budget gap through its own efforts or savings plans. This is a structural financial sustainability issue, not a one-off problem.
findings.figures: Council requested and received exceptional financial support to balance 2024/25 budget; 'still reliant on EFS to set a balanced budget' (2025/26 onwards)
findings.quote: As part of the 2024/25 budget setting process, the Council made a request for, and received, exceptional financial support from the Government in order to balance the budget for 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: Middlesbrough Council Audit Completion Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Auditor issuing disclaimed opinion: no assurance over financial statements
findings.detail: Forvis Mazars cannot complete audit procedures before the backstop date of 27 February 2026 and will issue a disclaimed opinion. This follows disclaimed opinions in 2023/24 and 2022/23. The auditor has no assurance over opening balances or the financial statements as a whole.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion means no independent verification of the council's financial position. For lenders, this removes a key source of assurance about the council's true financial state.
findings.figures: Three consecutive years of disclaimed opinions (2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24, and now 2024/25).
findings.quote: It has not been possible to complete sufficient procedures as part of the current year's audit to enable us to issue a non-disclaimed opinion. For this reason, we will be issuing a disclaimed opinion in time for the Council to publish its financial statements by the backstop date of 27 February 2026

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9 - Capital Programme and Strategy
findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio (Cleveland Centre, Captain Cook Precinct, Boho complex) has vacant units; £2m investment required to make spaces lettable and ensure compliance.
findings.detail: Council owns significant portfolio that is underperforming. "Inevitably there are / will be vacant units within the portfolio, which depending on current market conditions may not be entirely fit for tenant requirements." Some properties are "at an advanced age" requiring "periodic investment to ensure compliance with current safety legislation." Programme aims to "protect and enhance the income streams associated with the strategic commercial estate"—implying current income is under threat.
findings.matters: Portfolio underperformance and vacancy indicate the council's commercial property is not generating expected revenue. Further investment is required before units can be let, and future income is not assured in weak market conditions.
findings.figures: £2.0m investment in occupancy/compliance over 2026/27–2028/29; portfolio includes Cleveland Centre, Captain Cook Precinct, Centre Square Buildings 1 & 2, Boho complex
findings.quote: Inevitably there are / will be vacant units within the portfolio, which depending on current market conditions may not be entirely fit for tenant requirements... there is a need for a flexible capital allocation to allow for adaptation of space to enable lettings.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9 - Capital Programme and Strategy
findings.headline: Town Hall roof repair (£12m, 2027–2030) will force closure of concert venue and require relocation of registrar, creating revenue cost to be resolved through Medium Term Financial Plan refresh.
findings.detail: Three-year roof programme with concert hall closure from January 2027 to December 2027. "The relevant areas of the building will require complete closure whilst the works are being undertaken." "There will inevitably be a revenue cost due to the closure from lost income within the concert facility and potentially the Registrar's Office. This will be addressed as part of the Medium Term Financial Plan refresh." Revenue costs not yet quantified and will require budget headroom to absorb.
findings.matters: Capital project is creating new revenue costs (lost concert income, registrar relocation) that will compound existing budget pressures. Revenue impact is acknowledged but not yet quantified—deferred to budget refresh.
findings.figures: £12.0m capital cost; revenue cost amount TBD
findings.quote: There will inevitably be a revenue cost due to the closure from lost income within the concert facility and potentially the Registrar's Office. This will be addressed as part of the Medium Term Financial Plan refresh.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9 - Capital Programme and Strategy
findings.headline: Homelessness and temporary accommodation budgets "working to huge pressures" from national housing shortage, with £1m capital bid plus £6.1m of grants assigned to address statutory obligations.
findings.detail: Council states "Homeless temporary accommodation budgets are working to huge pressures as we see national housing pressures lack of suitable housing, increase in homelessness, increase in clients with support needs, reduced services and budgets to support vulnerable clients manifest within Middlesbrough placing pressure on our budgets and services." This is a statutory obligation (Homelessness Act 2002) that cannot be deferred, meaning ongoing structural pressure on revenue budget. Document notes "Whilst not the primary driver, preventing homelessness does reduce the burden on the Council's revenue resources"—implying the current revenue cost is material.
findings.matters: Homelessness costs are statutory, non-discretionary, and growing. This is a long-term drag on revenue budget that will absorb resources from other priorities or require continued borrowing.
findings.figures: £1.0m council capital bid; £6.141m grant and Section 106 contributions already assigned
findings.quote: Homeless temporary accommodation budgets are working to huge pressures as we see national housing pressures lack of suitable housing, increase in homelessness, increase in clients with support needs, reduced services and budgets to support vulnerable clients manifest within Middlesbrough placing pressure on our budgets and services.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9 - Capital Programme and Strategy
findings.headline: £7.059m of capital receipts being used to fund transformation and redundancy costs rather than capital assets, indicating revenue budget cannot absorb restructuring costs.
findings.detail: Council is using "Flexible Use of Capital Receipts" (£5.789m in 2026/27, £1.27m in 2027/28) to fund transformation programme and redundancy costs. This is a revenue-side use of capital receipts, which signals the revenue budget lacks capacity to fund restructuring from operations.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are a finite resource. Using them for transformation costs (rather than new capital investment) both depletes the asset base and signals underlying revenue deficit or severe budget pressure.
findings.figures: Flexible Use of Capital Receipts: 2026/27 £5.789m, 2027/28 £1.270m, total £7.059m
findings.quote: It also shows the level of capital receipts over the MTFP period. A Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Strategy for 2026/27 totaling £5.789m is attached at Appendix 10 for consideration and approval by Council on 18 February 2026

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9 - Capital Programme and Strategy
findings.headline: Capital receipts from asset sales depleting from £17.7m (2027/28) to £0 by 2029/30, eliminating future capital flexibility once current programme completes.
findings.detail: Council carried forward £13.25m in receipts from prior years and generates £22–15m annually, but consumes nearly all for capital investment. By 2029/30, all receipts are committed and carried-forward balance reaches zero. After 2030, council will have no capital receipt buffer and must rely entirely on borrowing, grants, or contributions for any future capital needs.
findings.matters: Signals exhaustion of the council's own resources and growing dependency on borrowing or external funding. If further asset maintenance emerges after 2030, borrowing will be the only option.
findings.quote: Capital receipts to carry forward 17.687... 15.659... 5.878... -

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9 - Capital Programme and Strategy
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increasing to £333.755m in 2026/27 (up from £312.383m), with external borrowing rising to £326.028m to fund £70.1m of the capital programme.
findings.detail: Total capital programme £183.7m over four years, with borrowing accounting for 38% (£70.1m). CFR rising £21.4m in one year. Debt servicing costs 7.1–8.4% of net revenue budget. External borrowing increasing £36.7m. Over-reliance on borrowing to fund capital investment.
findings.matters: Significant acceleration in the council's debt position. With debt servicing already consuming 7–8% of revenue budget (a material share of constrained finances), rising borrowing is a key risk to financial resilience.
findings.quote: The Council's Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) is the underlying need to borrow in relation to historical borrowing plus future planned borrowing to fund the Council's capital investment in assets. This is expected to increase to £333.755m in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9 - Capital Programme and Strategy
findings.headline: £35.1m of urgent deferred maintenance now being fast-tracked, including £12m Town Hall roof, £10m highway overbridge, and £6m council depot repairs.
findings.detail: Multiple buildings and infrastructure previously deferred due to affordability constraints are now urgent. Town Hall roof is "of an urgent nature and cannot be further delayed." Longlands Road overbridge has had "progressive deterioration" despite temporary fixes since the 1970s and risks "unplanned closure." Council depot in "significant state of disrepair" requiring complete roof replacement and refurbishment. Neptune Centre roofing "at risk of lifting in high winds, which will cause significant damage to the building structure, surrounding buildings and a high-level risk to the public."
findings.matters: Reveals a backlog of deferred maintenance that was previously absorbed rather than managed. Suggests the capital investment plan is partially driven by crisis rather than strategic choice, limiting flexibility for new investment.
findings.figures: Town Hall £12.0m, Longlands Road overbridge £10.0m, Cargo Fleet Depot £6.0m, Neptune Centre £1.8m, Dorman Museum £1.325m, Broadcasting House £1.5m
findings.quote: This work has been deferred previously as a consequence of affordability and disruption to services. However, the work is now of an urgent nature and cannot be further delayed.

findings.paper_title: 18-2-26 Council - PI Annual Treasury Management Report 2026-27 FINAL
findings.headline: Elected members have not received formal treasury training since 2021; a gap of 5+ years in oversight of decisions involving £350m+ of debt and £14m+ annual financing costs
findings.detail: The council states formal treasury training by external advisers 'was undertaken in 2021' and notes it 'is good practice to have regular specialist training in this area due to the complexity of the subject matter and the high levels of risk involved.' New training is being arranged, but the gap signals a potential governance weakness during a period of debt expansion and affordability uncertainty.
findings.matters: Complex treasury decisions involving large debt, volatile interest rates, and uncertain affordability thresholds benefit from informed member scrutiny. A 5-year gap in specialist training may have left members under-equipped to question strategy or identify risks.
findings.figures: External debt £269.360m (Dec 2025); annual financing costs £14.151m (2026/27 forecast)
findings.quote: The last formal training in this area provided by our external advisers was undertaken in 2021. However, it is good practice to have regular specialist training in this area due to the complexity of the subject matter and the high levels of risk involved in treasury matters. A session is therefore being organised between Arlingclose and Members to be held prior to the Council meeting on 18 February 2026.

findings.paper_title: 18-2-26 Council - PI Annual Treasury Management Report 2026-27 FINAL
findings.headline: Capital receipts from asset disposals are central to the financing strategy and have 'increased significantly'; £22.2m is forecast for 2026/27 alone
findings.detail: The capital programme depends on generating substantial receipts from asset sales. The council notes receipts 'have increased significantly in recent years due to the asset review undertaken by the Council' and uses a 'Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Policy' to fund transformation costs. If the asset disposal programme slips, the council would need to either cut capital or increase borrowing.
findings.matters: The financing plan is contingent on executing a large asset sales programme on schedule. Slippage would force difficult choices between reduced capital investment, higher debt, or use of reserves.
findings.figures: Capital receipts forecast: £22.186m (2026/27), £15.302m (2027/28); total capital expenditure 2026/27 £79.483m
findings.quote: These amounts have increased significantly in recent years due to the asset review undertaken by the Council. Some of these receipts may not be required in the financial year they are generated and can be carried forward for future use.

findings.paper_title: 18-2-26 Council - PI Annual Treasury Management Report 2026-27 FINAL
findings.headline: External debt is forecast to rise from £289.36m to £351.23m over four years—a £61.87m increase—despite the council already having reached borrowing affordability limits
findings.detail: The council plans to increase external debt by over £60m through 2030 to fund capital investment, with the bulk borrowed from the Public Works Loan Board (89% of current borrowing) at rates of 4.25–6.25%. This expansion follows a period when the council was already at the limit of what it could afford to service from revenue.
findings.matters: Material debt escalation in a constrained affordability environment, particularly dependent on property income and asset sales, signals elevated refinance risk and limited capacity to absorb financial shocks.
findings.figures: External debt: £289.360m (31 Mar 2026), £351.233m (31 Mar 2030); long-term PWLB rates 4.25–6.25%
findings.quote: The forecast overall total long term external debt at the end of 2025/26 is therefore £289.360 million and should be compared with the estimated Capital Financing Requirement (the underlying value which the Council needs to borrow to fund capital activities) of £312.383 million.

findings.paper_title: 18-2-26 Council - PI Annual Treasury Management Report 2026-27 FINAL
findings.headline: £2.6m annual commercial property rental income is flagged as a key budget risk; if rental levels fall, the council's debt affordability will be directly undermined
findings.detail: The council's financing costs forecast includes approximately £2.6m of income from commercial property investments. The report states this explicitly: 'It is imperative and a key budget risk that these rental levels are maintained, and the income assumed in the estimates above continue to be generated.' This signals narrow headroom and exposure to property market downturn.
findings.matters: The council's ability to service growing debt (forecast to reach £351m) depends on holding specific rental income. A market downturn, tenant defaults, or portfolio deterioration could create a shortfall with limited alternative funding sources.
findings.figures: £2.6m annual rental income; total financing costs 2026/27 £14.151m; external debt forecast to reach £351.233m by 2030
findings.quote: It is imperative and a key budget risk that these rental levels are maintained, and the income assumed in the estimates above continue to be generated.

findings.paper_title: 18-2-26 Council - PI Annual Treasury Management Report 2026-27 FINAL
findings.headline: Council was at the limit of revenue affordability on borrowing, but the Fair Funding Review 2.0 has changed net revenue budget calculations, leaving the new affordability threshold uncertain
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it was reaching the limit of affordability for debt-funded capital investment. However, the recent Local Government Finance Settlement changes have made pre-2026/27 figures non-comparable. The council now needs to review whether the 10% CIPFA affordability benchmark still applies under the new methodology, creating uncertainty about its true debt capacity.
findings.matters: Lenders rely on affordability metrics to assess default risk. A council that was already at capacity, facing a recalibration of those metrics and unable yet to confirm the new ceiling, is taking on escalating debt against an unquantified constraint.
findings.figures: Financing costs as % of net revenue budget: 8.5% (2025/26 forecast); 7.0% (2026/27 forecast)
findings.quote: Whilst the Council is not an outlier in terms of its level of total debt, it was reaching the limit of its revenue affordability on borrowing to fund its future capital investment. Changes to the Local Government Finance Settlement and how the net revenue budget have been calculated have changed significantly with the Fair Funding Review 2.0 and are not now comparable post the 2026/27 budget. The Council will need to review what the affordability threshold will be in this context and if the 10% best practice amount previously recommended by CIPFA is still relevant.

findings.headline: Children's Care demand surge from case complexity and external residential placements totalling £10.584m over four years
findings.detail: External residential placements for children are driving sustained demand pressure of £3.0m per year 2026/27–2028/29, then £1.5m in 2029/30. The paper explicitly cites increased case complexity as a driver. This sits alongside £0.084m for S17 emergency accommodation and legal/financial support.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Forecast Service Demand Pressures and Re-basing of Budgets
findings.headline: Adult Social Care cost escalation driven by National Living Wage and legal/demand pressures totalling £17.754m over four years
findings.detail: The single largest budget pressure is adult social care, with £8.277m from National Living Wage effects on commissioned services alone. Multiple statutory requirements are creating new costs: Mental Capacity Assessments (£0.131m), Mental Health Act provisions for learning disabilities (£0.150m), Mental Health Act advocacy opt-out changes (£0.080m), and annual care package reviews (£0.216m). Base demand is rising £2.020m in 2026/27 and £1.5m annually thereafter.
findings.matters: Adult social care typically consumes 20%+ of a council's budget; this shows structural cost escalation from both external factors (living wage) and regulatory requirements with no clear funding solution.
findings.figures: £17.754m cumulative (£6.782m, £3.548m, £3.691m, £3.733m across years). Living Wage impact alone £8.277m. Individual statutory requirements £0.131m–£0.216m each.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5 - Indicative Net Revenue Budget by Directorate 2026-27
findings.headline: Adult Social Care budget increases 21.8% to £67.4m, making it the council's largest single directorate
findings.detail: Adult Social Care & Health grows from £55.264m to £67.373m, an increase of £12.1m year-on-year. This directorate absorbs the largest block of the council's revenue spending and is growing faster than overall budget growth, indicating concentrated structural cost pressure.
findings.matters: Adult Social Care is now the council's single largest cost area and its 22% growth reflects sector-wide demand and staffing pressures that directly affect the council's financial sustainability and affordability.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5 - Indicative Net Revenue Budget by Directorate 2026-27
findings.headline: Budget allocations remain unsettled, with significant changes pending management restructure before Council sign-off on 18/02/26
findings.detail: The document is explicitly marked indicative and subject to change. The council notes that allocations will change because 'FULL EFFECT OF SERVICE MOVES DUE TO SENIOR MANAGEMENT REVIEW CURRENTLY NOT REFLECTED AND SOME ALLOCATIONS ARE STILL SUBJECT TO FURTHER WORK/ANALYSIS'. This means the current figures are incomplete.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence in a council's settled budget and service model. Unresolved allocations pending an internal restructure signals that the council's financial structure is not yet finalised, creating near-term uncertainty.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Proposed revenue budget virements above £250,000 at Quarter One 2025-26
findings.headline: Planned £250k residents parking charging saving did not proceed
findings.detail: The council had budgeted to save £250k through introducing residents' parking charges (saving ECS08), but this scheme is no longer going ahead with charging. The shortfall is being covered by the central contingency budget for 2025-26, indicating the council had to absorb this revenue loss from contingency reserves.
findings.matters: A planned revenue-raising initiative failed to materialise, indicating either operational or political constraints; reliance on contingency to cover the £250k gap shows pressure on the base budget and suggests limited headroom for unplanned pressures.
